text: The equal-weight view of peer disagreement (Elga, Christensen, Feldman) recommends that, on discovering that a recognized epistemic peer disagrees with you, you should:
choices: give your peer's conclusion the same evidential weight as your own and revise your credence toward theirs, roughly splitting the difference.
retain your original credence unchanged, provided your first-order evidence in fact supported your conclusion.
infer that the two of you were never genuine epistemic peers, since genuine peers do not persist in disagreement.
attend only to your total first-order evidence about the disputed question and disregard the fact of disagreement as mere noise.
explanation: The equal-weight version of conciliationism treats the peer's contrary judgment as evidence of the same force as your own, so you move your credence toward theirs (split the difference). Option 1 is the steadfast or right-reasons view (Kelly); option 2 is the Sosa-style claim that apparent peer disagreement usually reveals that the parties were not genuine peers; option 3 mischaracterizes total-evidence views. Only option 0 states the equal-weight recommendation.
